The one-off exception ate the anchor. A biweekly series has a parity - this Friday yes, next Friday no - and the parity lives entirely in the anchor date. When the holiday payday was implemented by moving the series, every subsequent occurrence was regenerated from the moved date, which flipped the parity permanently: the series now runs on the opposite set of Fridays, forever, and each individual payday looks like a one-week error.

The mechanical rule is that occurrences must always be generated from the original anchor, never from the previous occurrence and never from an adjusted occurrence. An exception - this one payday moves to Thursday - is a fact about one occurrence, stored as an override attached to that date. The generator asks "what does the rule say for this date, and is there an override?" It never asks "when was the last payday?" because the last payday might itself have been an exception, and chaining from exceptions compounds them.

It is the same defect as the subscription that renews on the 31st, slides to February 28, and then renews on the 28th forever: anchor rot. Anywhere a recurrence is computed from its own previous output, a single clamp, holiday, or manual nudge becomes the new reality. The fix for payroll is to restore the January anchor in configuration, store the holiday Thursday as a one-date override, and add a test that would have caught this: generate a year of paydays and assert every one is a Friday on the anchor's parity, with overrides listed explicitly rather than absorbed.

The 365-day rule drifts off the anniversary entirely and, most quietly, never returns to February 29 - in 2028, a leap year when the true anniversary exists, it lands on February 28, a day early, forever. The roll-forward rule has the mirror flaw: having rolled to March 1 once, it is anchored to March 1 for good. But "usually safe" is not a policy. The decision - which rule, and whether early or late is the acceptable error - belongs to whoever owns the compliance obligation, and it must be written down, because the three tools in your stack have already voted three different ways.

The generalizable point: every recurrence rule needs its edge policy stated for the impossible dates - February 29, the 31st of a 30-day month, the nonexistent 02:30. Libraries each have a default, the defaults disagree, and the disagreement surfaces years later, on exactly the dates nobody tests.

Take the intervals between consecutive occurrences, in seconds, and look at their pattern. A constant interval - every gap exactly 604,800 seconds for a weekly event, or exactly 2,592,000 for a 30-day one - is an interval rule anchored to an instant. It will also show its local readings wandering across DST transitions, because the instant is fixed and the readings are not.

If the local readings are constant instead - always 09:00 on the same wall clock - while the intervals wobble by an hour around March and November (601,200 and 608,400 seconds for a weekly event), it is a wall-clock rule: the zone-anchored kind a calendar system produces.

A day that degrades and never recovers (31, 28, 28, 28) means the rule chains from the previous occurrence - anchor rot, visible in the fossil record. A day that walks steadily earlier (31, 2, 1, 1, 31...) with constant 30-day intervals means it was never a monthly rule at all.

Two years is plenty: you need only one DST transition and one February to distinguish most of the candidates. Reconstruct the rule, write it down as the system's actual specification, and then decide - with the history as evidence - whether the rule it implements is the rule the business believes it bought. The gap between those two is where recurrence bugs live.

Every-28-days is a four-week rule, and months are not four weeks: they are 28 to 31 days, so a fixed 28-day cycle slips against the calendar by two or three days a month, compounding. By March the shortcut and the rule still coincide, which feels like confirmation. By April the shortcut is holding the "first Monday" meeting on March 30 - the fifth Monday of March, in the wrong month entirely for a monthly governance meeting - and by November it is a week late against the real first Monday.

The deeper problem is that the shortcut answers a different question. "Every 28 days" is an interval rule; "first Monday of the month" is a calendar rule defined by position within a month. They agree only when the calendar happens to cooperate, and they disagree most in exactly the months with five Mondays, which are the months a board is likeliest to care about.

Calendar rules must be computed from the calendar: take the first of the month, advance to the first Monday, repeat per month from the anchor rule - never from the previous occurrence. The general audit you can run on any recurrence in your systems: generate a year from the implementation and a year from the stated rule, and diff them. If they differ, one of them is the real specification, and it is usually the implementation - which is why the code must be brought back to the stated rule, with the diff as the test that keeps it there.
We keep having recurrence bugs - drifting billing dates, meetings that move, a review that landed on the wrong day. Is there a checklist we can apply when anyone implements a new recurrence?

Yes - five decisions, made in writing, before the code. Most recurrence bugs are not coding errors; they are decisions nobody made, discovered later by customers.

One: the anchor. Every recurrence hangs from an explicit anchor - a date or instant, stored in configuration, that occurrences are generated from. Never generate from the previous occurrence; that is how one clamp or holiday becomes permanent.

Two: the rule type. Is this an interval (every 30 days, every 6 hours - elapsed time, indifferent to calendars) or a calendar rule (monthly on the 31st, first Monday, every Friday)? The two families have different arithmetic, different failure modes, and different honest names. If the business says "monthly," the rule is calendar.

Three: the zone, for anything with a wall-clock meaning. A recurrence without a named zone is a recurrence that will be interpreted in whatever zone the next server happens to run in.

Four: the edge policy. What happens on the impossible dates - the 31st in February, February 29 in a common year, 02:30 on spring-forward day, 01:30 twice on fall-back day? Clamp, roll, skip, fire-twice: any is defensible, none may be left to a library's default, because the libraries disagree with each other.

Five: who absorbs daylight saving. For a multi-zone event, name the anchor zone; the other zones will move twice a year and the invitation should say so.

Write those five lines next to the code, and generate one year of occurrences as a test fixture, diffed against a hand-checked list that includes a February and both transition weeks. A recurrence that has survived that fixture has had its decisions made. One that has not is a bug report scheduled for a date you cannot predict - which is, at least, on-brand.

A legacy events table has an epoch column that turns out to contain a mix of seconds, milliseconds, and microseconds - different writers over the years used different units. The events are known to span 2025-01-01 to 2027-12-31. Values include 1735689600, 1767225600, 1767225600000, 1767225600000000, 1798761600, 1798761600000, 12345678901, and 999999999999. Triage them.

Six of the eight values repair cleanly, and the magnitude bands do the work: for events in this era, epoch seconds are ten digits, milliseconds thirteen, microseconds sixteen, and the three populations do not overlap. Note the quiet confirmation in the output - three different raw values, one in each unit, all land on exactly 2026-01-01 00:00Z. Independent writers recording the same New Year event in different units is the kind of coincidence that validates the whole classification.

The other two values are where honesty matters. 12345678901 fits the seconds band, but read as seconds it names a date in the year 2361 - outside the dataset's known span, so the band's answer cannot be trusted; it goes to review, not into the repaired column. And 999999999999 fits no band at all: too large for seconds in any plausible era, too small for milliseconds. Values in that gap are the genuinely ambiguous ones - they would be milliseconds for a 2001 event or seconds for a year-33658 event, and for this dataset they are neither, so they are quarantined rather than assigned.

The method generalizes: classify by magnitude, convert, then validate against everything you know about the dataset - its span, its expected event density, its known landmarks. A conversion that survives all three checks is a repair. One that fails any check is a question, and the repaired table should carry a flag saying which rows are which.

We're about to repair five years of mixed-unit, mixed-format timestamps. My instinct is to write one big migration that fixes the column in place so it's clean. A colleague is arguing for new columns and flags. Why is she right?

Because a repair is an interpretation, and interpretations need to be revisable. Your in-place migration takes values whose meaning you have inferred - from magnitude bands, from writer eras, from anchors - and overwrites the evidence with the conclusion. If one inference is wrong (and across five years of mixed data, one will be), there is no way back: the original bytes are gone, the error is undetectable, and every downstream number built on it is quietly contaminated.

Her design keeps the raw column untouched and adds three things: a normalized instant column, a rule column naming how each row was interpreted (unit-seconds, format-EU, writer-era-Denver, anchor-verified), and a confidence or status marker (repaired, inferred, quarantined). That buys you four concrete things. A better-informed future repair - say a config file surfaces next year proving an era's zone - can redo exactly the affected rows. An auditor can sample the repairs rule by rule. A disputed row can be traced to its raw value in one step. And quarantined rows stay visible as a counted, owned problem instead of being laundered into plausible-looking data.

The cost is real: more columns, consumers must choose which to read, and the table never looks "clean." But clean was never the actual goal - trustworthy is. A timestamp column that everyone believes and nobody can verify is worse than a messy one with its reasoning attached. Migrations that destroy evidence to achieve tidiness are how organizations end up unable to answer simple questions about their own history.

How bad is the all-numeric date ambiguity problem really, at scale? Our merged table has about 200,000 rows in MM/DD or DD/MM with no provenance on most of them. Leadership wants a number for how many rows are at risk before they fund a cleanup.

Here is the number and how to derive it for your table. A row is at risk exactly when both numbers are 12 or under - the day is 12 or less, so the string parses under both formats and means two different dates (or, rarely, the same one). For a roughly uniform spread of real dates, the fraction of days in a year whose day-of-month is 12 or less is 12 out of an average month length of about 30.4 - so expect about 39% of your rows, roughly 79,000 of the 200,000, to be two-faced in principle. Subtract the small share where both numbers are equal ("07/07") and the date is the same either way - about 3% of the at-risk set - and you land near 76,000 rows whose true date cannot be recovered from the string alone.

That is the honest headline: not "the column is a bit messy" but "about 38% of this table's dates are unknowable from the data itself." It reframes the funding conversation correctly, because the cleanup is not a parsing project. The provable 62% can be converted mechanically in an afternoon. The at-risk rows need evidence from outside the column: source files, import logs, neighboring columns (a created-at timestamp, a sequential ID whose order correlates with date), or the counterparties who sent the records. Some fraction will be recoverable by provenance archaeology; the rest are permanently ambiguous and should be flagged as such rather than resolved by a default.

One more number for leadership: any analysis already run over this column has silently picked one format - whatever the parsing library defaulted to - so historical reports that group by these dates carry errors concentrated in that same 38%. The cleanup budget should include re-running the ones anyone still believes.

from datetime import datetime

CURRENT_YEAR = 2026
SYSTEM_EPOCH = 2020   # the licensing system went live in 2020

def pivot(s):
    return datetime.strptime(s, "%m/%d/%y").date()

print("birthdates, standard pivot:")
for s in ["03/15/45", "07/04/68", "11/26/15", "01/30/99", "05/09/30"]:
    d = pivot(s)
    verdict = "plausible" if d.year <= CURRENT_YEAR else "FUTURE birthdate - flip century"
    fixed = d.replace(year=d.year - 100) if d.year > CURRENT_YEAR else d
    print(f"  {s} -> {d}  {verdict}  (use {fixed})")

print()
print("license renewals, standard pivot:")
for s in ["03/15/30", "07/04/68"]:
    d = pivot(s)
    verdict = "plausible" if d.year >= SYSTEM_EPOCH else "before the system existed - flip century"
    fixed = d.replace(year=d.year + 100) if d.year < SYSTEM_EPOCH else d
    print(f"  {s} -> {d}  {verdict}  (use {fixed})")

The standard pivot is a reasonable default for documents written near the present, and it breaks exactly where a column's semantics push dates far from the present in either direction. In the birthdates it manufactures three people who have not been born yet: "45" becomes 2045, "68" becomes 2068, and "30" becomes 2030, and a pipeline that does not check will happily compute negative ages for customers born in 1945, 1968, and 1930. The birthdate rule is a plausibility window - a birthdate cannot be in the future - so any parsed year after the current year flips back a century.

The renewal table reads the very same strings and must keep what the birthdates reject. "07/04/68" as a renewal is 2068 - a license expiring four decades out is ordinary - and flipping it the birthdate way would manufacture a renewal dated 1968, decades before the licensing system existed. "03/15/30" likewise stays 2030. The two tables need opposite treatment of identical bytes because the plausibility windows face opposite directions: birthdates are bounded above by today, renewals are bounded below by the system's birth and expected to run into the future.

The lesson is that a two-digit year is not a date with a formatting quirk; it is a date with a century missing, and the century is supplied by the column's meaning, not by a global constant. Every column gets its own plausibility window - birthdates bounded above by today, renewals bounded below by the system's birth, transactions bounded by the company's existence - and the pivot is just the first guess the window then corrects. And when you repair, record the rule per column. The next person to see "68" in both tables deserves to know why it became 1968 in one and 2068 in the other.

We're repairing naive timestamps from 2005-2007 that we believe were written in New York local time. A junior engineer wrote a converter that applies 'EST = UTC-5, EDT = UTC-4, DST from the second Sunday of March'. I stopped him before he ran it. Was I right?

You were right, and the reason is subtle enough to be worth teaching him rather than just stopping him. His converter applies the rules of 2026 to the readings of 2005 - but the United States changed its DST rules in 2007. Before 2007, daylight time ran from the first Sunday of April to the last Sunday of October. In 2005 and 2006 there are three weeks of March, and a week at the end of October, where his converter assigns the wrong offset: it would read a March 20, 2006 morning timestamp as EDT when New York was still on EST, shifting the repaired instant by an hour for every row in those windows.

The general principle: a timezone is not a pair of offsets; it is a history of rules, and the rules themselves change - legislatures move DST dates, countries abolish DST entirely, regions switch zones. The tz database that zoneinfo reads is a historical document: it knows that New York in March 2006 followed the pre-2007 rules, and converting a 2006 reading with ZoneInfo("America/New_York") applies the era's rules automatically. Hand-rolled offset tables encode the rules of the year the programmer happened to write them, applied to every year indiscriminately.

This cuts both ways, and the second direction matters for recent data too: a converter written from memory ("Phoenix is UTC-7") happens to be safe, but the same style of converter for a region that changed its rules recently - and several have, in both directions, in the last decade - corrupts quietly. The rule for repairs: always convert through the tz database with the zone's name, never through an offset table, and be most suspicious of the repairs that look simplest.

Different repair problem: one column, one writer, but the writer switched from epoch seconds to epoch milliseconds at a migration in the middle of the table's history. The rows are in ingest order. How do I find the switch point and repair the column?

Use the ingest order - it is the one piece of structure the unit change cannot hide in. Take the values in order and look at their magnitudes on a log scale: seconds for this era are ten-digit numbers, milliseconds are thirteen-digit, so the series sits on one plateau, steps up by a factor of a thousand at the migration, and stays there. The switch point is the row where the step happens, and in practice it is unmissable once you look at the data in order rather than in aggregate. An aggregate view - a histogram of the whole column - just shows you two humps and no idea which rows belong to which era.

Verify the step before trusting it: convert the rows just before the step as seconds and the rows just after it as milliseconds, and check that the resulting instants are continuous across the boundary - the last seconds-row and the first milliseconds-row should be minutes or hours apart, not centuries. Also check monotonicity: a healthy event stream converted with the right per-era units is non-decreasing in ingest order; any remaining sawtooth means a pocket of rows the simple two-era story does not explain (a backfill, a replayed batch) and those rows get individual attention.

Two warnings. First, never sort the raw column before repairing it: sorted by raw value, the milliseconds rows all land after the seconds rows regardless of when the events happened, and you will have manufactured a false chronology that looks clean. Repair in ingest order, then sort by the repaired instant. Second, the step method works because the eras are contiguous; if the migration was gradual - two writers overlapping for a month - there is no single step, and the boundary rows need the writer-level provenance treatment instead. Look at the shape of the transition before choosing the tool.
I found a column called 'elapsed' typed as a timestamp. Every value is on the same date in 1970 and the times cluster between 00:00 and 06:00. What am I looking at?

You are looking at durations that someone stored as times of day. A job that took 90 minutes got written as 01:30:00; a job that took 5 hours 41 minutes became 05:41:00 - the elapsed seconds were formatted, or cast, into a time type, and the date part is the epoch's birthday, January 1, 1970, because that is what a duration of zero looks like when you force it into a timestamp.

The cluster between 00:00 and 06:00 is the distribution of your job runtimes wearing a costume: most jobs take under six hours. If any job ever ran longer than 24 hours you will find its duration wrapped - a 26-hour job stored as 02:00 on January 2, or truncated to 02:00 on January 1 - and those rows are worth hunting specifically, because a wrapped duration is indistinguishable from a short one without outside evidence.

The conversion back is mechanical: extract the seconds since the epoch-midnight the value pretends to be - hours times 3600 plus minutes times 60 plus seconds - and store that as a duration in a properly typed column. But do not stop at the conversion, because the column is also a process finding: somewhere upstream, a duration and a timestamp were treated as interchangeable, and that confusion is rarely confined to one field. Search the schema for other duration-shaped data in time-shaped columns (columns named *_at that contain 1970 dates are the classic tell), and add the general rule to your data standards: a timestamp answers "when," a duration answers "how long," and a column's type must say which question it answers.

A best guess written into a timestamp column stops being a guess the moment it lands. Downstream, it is indistinguishable from a measured value: it gets averaged, ordered, windowed, and cited, and nobody - including you, in six months - can tell which rows were evidence and which were invented to fill a gap. The dashboard's gap is not a cosmetic flaw; it is the data telling the truth about what the organization knows. Filling it with guesses does not remove the ignorance, it removes the visibility of the ignorance, which is the only part that was protecting every future decision.

The costs are concrete. One guessed era boundary can shift a cohort's worth of rows by hours and reverse an ordering conclusion. A guessed format on an ambiguous date is wrong about half the time by construction. And when a guess is later discovered - they always are, usually by an auditor or an angry counterparty - the discovery contaminates the whole table: if these rows were invented, why should anyone trust the rest?

Offer the alternative that solves his actual problem: keep the gaps, but make them first-class. A null instant with a quality flag renders in dashboards as "unrecorded," which is a presentable, honest category - finance and compliance audiences accept "we cannot establish when" far more readily than they accept a discovered fabrication. If a dashboard needs a continuous series, let it impute at display time, labeled as imputed, where the guess is visible and disposable. Guesses belong in the presentation layer, where they can be seen. In the data layer, they are just lies with good intentions.

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

PHOENIX = ZoneInfo("America/Phoenix")   # UTC-7 all year; Arizona skips DST

    print(f"  {oid}: purchase {purchase:%H:%M}Z, refund reading {reading}")

Phoenix is the friendly version of this bug, incidentally - Arizona does not observe daylight saving, so its offset is UTC-7 in every month and the reconciliation is a single constant. The same export from a Denver or Chicago tool would reconcile in winter and break in summer, and the analyst would trust it precisely because it had been right for months.

The forensic sequence to teach from this case: before concluding an event order is impossible, establish the provenance of every timestamp in the comparison - who wrote it, in what zone, from which clock - then convert everything to one scale, and only then reason about order. And the systemic fix is the familiar one: the partner feed's contract must carry offsets, because a timestamp without a zone is a rumor, and this analyst nearly filed a fraud report about a rumor.
We're about to write up a major incident where the timestamps disagreed across systems. Before I draft it: what does a good forensic time report actually contain?

Five sections, in this order, and the order is the discipline.

Provenance first, conclusions last. For every timestamp source in the incident, establish who wrote it - which service, on which host, in which configured zone, from which clock, and whether that configuration changed during the incident window. This section is a table, not a narrative, and it comes before any timeline because every later claim depends on it. A report that opens with a timeline built from unexamined timestamps is fiction with good formatting.

Then the canonical timeline: every event converted to one scale - UTC instants - in true order, with each entry showing the original reading alongside its source and zone, so a reader can audit every conversion. Entries whose placement is inferred rather than recorded are marked as inferred. Gaps are stated as gaps ("no source covers 02:10-02:40") rather than smoothed over.

Then the reconciliation: the specific conversions that dissolved the apparent contradictions - the refund that preceded its purchase until Phoenix was applied, the duplicate that was a fold. This is the section that teaches; it should show at least the headline arithmetic, not just assert it.

Then the fix, stated as changes to how timestamps are produced and stored, not as exhortations to be careful: store instants, carry offsets in feed contracts, name zones in schedules.

Finally, the audit that catches the next one: the query, alert, or test that would have flagged this disagreement before an incident did. A report without that section is a story; with it, it is a control.

I'm building the timeline exhibit for an incident review. The sources disagree, some entries are inferred, and there are gaps. How do I present it so it survives scrutiny from people who were not there?

Build it as an exhibit, not a narrative - the standard is that a skeptical reader can re-derive every line.

One spine: UTC, instants only, strictly ordered. Every other representation is a column, never the sort key. Each row carries four things: the UTC instant; the original reading exactly as recorded, with its source and zone ("app-2 log, 01:12, host configured America/New_York"); the event; and a basis marker distinguishing recorded from inferred. An inferred entry says what it is inferred from ("placed between the deploy confirmation and the first error, from the 40-second deploy duration in the runbook") - inference with its reasoning attached is evidence; inference dressed as a record is a liability.

Gaps get rows of their own: "02:10-02:40Z - no source covers this window; the metrics host was down." A stated gap is a fact about your knowledge and often the most useful line in the exhibit, because it tells the review where to stop drawing conclusions. The temptation to bridge gaps with plausible connective tissue is how incident reviews manufacture false causes.

Two more disciplines. Where two sources disagree about the same event, both readings appear, with the disagreement named and your resolution argued in a note - never silently pick the one that fits the story. And conversions are shown, not performed invisibly: a reader who wants to check that the Phoenix refund really is 17:00Z should find the offset and the arithmetic in a footnote, not have to trust you.

Close the exhibit with the provenance table it rests on. If the exhibit survives, it will be because someone hostile to your conclusion tried to break a row and could not.

Next time we have a timestamp-mystery incident, I want the team to establish provenance fast instead of arguing from the logs. What are the questions, exactly?

Six, and they are asked of every timestamp source before anyone is allowed to interpret a reading.

One: who writes it? The application, the framework's default logger, the database, the load balancer, a partner's export? Each has its own defaults, and "the system" is not an answer.

Two: in which process, on which host? The answer locates the configuration that produced the value - and incidents regularly involve two services on the same host writing in different zones because one was configured and one inherited.

Three: from which clock? The host's system clock, synced how, with what health - and is the value a wall reading or a monotonic-derived one? A source with a sick clock poisons everything downstream of it.

Four: under which zone configuration, and in what format? Zone name or bare offset or nothing; and if nothing, the writing code's convention - established from the code, not from vibes.

Five: since when, and what changed inside the incident window? A re-image, a config push, a library upgrade, a migration. Most provenance mysteries resolve here: the values before the change mean one thing and after it another, and the incident window straddles the change.

Six: who else reads it, and what do they assume? Half of timestamp incidents are born at a boundary where the writer's convention and the reader's assumption differ, each perfectly consistent on its own side.

Write the answers into a provenance table at the top of the incident doc before the timeline is drafted. The questions take twenty minutes when asked on purpose. Asked accidentally, one at a time, in a chat thread, under pressure, they take the whole incident.

A backup job is defined as '00:00 server-local'. The server was re-imaged last month and its timezone changed from the office's zone to UTC in the process. The job now runs during the evening peak and the team swears 'nothing about the job changed'. Walk me through how you'd prove what happened.

Start by agreeing with them: nothing about the job changed, and that is precisely the problem. "00:00 server-local" is not a time; it is a reference to a configuration that lives outside the job. The re-image changed the referent, so the same definition now names a different instant - five or more hours earlier in UTC terms, landing in the previous local evening, on top of the peak. The job is a pointer, and someone moved what it points at.

The proof does not need the old server, because the filesystem kept the receipts. File timestamps - the modification times of the backup outputs - are stored as epoch instants, unambiguous, indifferent to anyone's zone settings. Pull the mtimes of the last few months of backup files and render each one twice: in UTC and in the office zone. Before the re-image, the office-zone renderings read 00:0x and the UTC renderings read 05:0x. After it, the renderings swap: UTC reads 00:0x and the office zone reads 19:0x the previous day. The step in the series sits exactly on the re-image date, and each regime is perfectly regular on its own side - the signature of a definition whose meaning changed, not of a job that drifted or failed.

Then close the loop on prevention. The job definition should never have been able to change meaning silently: schedules get named zones ("00:00 America/New_York") or explicit UTC, chosen by intent - a backup tied to the business day wants the office zone named, a backup tied to a global quiet window wants UTC. And a re-image checklist that includes "host timezone" would have caught this in advance, because the host's zone is configuration that other systems are silently depending on.
Give me the fix-pattern catalog for time bugs - the short list of rules I can hand a team, each tied to the failure it prevents.

Seven rules. Each exists because a specific, recurring failure paid for it.

Store instants, render locally. Timestamps are stored as UTC instants with offsets preserved at capture; zones are applied at display and at window boundaries only. Prevents: every naive-versus-aware mix, every "refund before purchase," every month that changes when re-zoned.

A timestamp without a zone is a rumor. Any feed, export, or log that carries a wall reading must name its zone or offset in the contract, and consumers reject unlabeled readings. Prevents: provenance mysteries, partner-feed reconciliations, fold-night duplicates.

Name the zone in every schedule and every window definition. "Daily 02:30" and "monthly" are unfinished sentences; "02:30 America/New_York" and "calendar month, Europe/Berlin" are specifications. Prevents: jobs drifting against business intent, SLA reports that disagree with the contract.

Compare timestamps from one clock, or budget the skew. Cross-machine ordering claims carry a tolerance; inside the tolerance, the honest verdict is "indistinguishable." Prevents: future requests, phantom causality violations, impossible sequences that are really clock differences.

Durations come from monotonic clocks. Wall clocks are calendars; they are stepped and slewed by design. Prevents: timeouts that fire instantly or never, negative latencies, TTLs that expire an hour early on the best night of the year.

Recurrences carry a contract: anchor, rule type, zone, edge policy, DST absorber. Prevents: 30-day "monthly" plans, first-Monday shortcuts, anchors that rot.

Repairs keep the raw value, the rule applied, and a confidence marker. Prevents: irreversible migrations, guesses hardening into facts, audits that cannot retrace a single row.

Pin the list where the team plans work. Time bugs are rarely knowledge problems - everyone on the team knows most of this. They are default problems, and defaults are set by whatever is written on the wall.

Last thing: our incident reviews keep ending with 'timestamps are hard'. I want a closing checklist instead - the questions we ask of any timestamp before we trust it. Give me the list.

Five questions. Tape them to the incident template.

Whose clock? The value came from a specific machine's clock, with a specific sync state. If you cannot name the machine and its clock health, the value's precision is unknown - treat its last digits as decoration.

Which zone? The reading was produced under a zone configuration - named, offset, or absent. Absent does not mean UTC; it means unestablished, and unestablished means the value cannot be compared with anything until it is.

Which era's rules? Zones are histories. The offset for a given zone differs by date, and the rules themselves have changed within living memory. Convert with the tz database, which knows the history, never with a remembered offset, which knows one year of it.

Instant or wall reading? An instant can be ordered, subtracted, and windowed. A wall reading is a label on a calendar page - ambiguous twice a year in fold, nonexistent once a year in the gap, and meaningless for ordering until it is married to a zone and a fold decision. Half of all timestamp incidents are this question, unasked.

Raw or repaired - and if repaired, by whom, under what rule? A repaired value carries its rule and its confidence, or it is a guess wearing a uniform. Quarantined and unknown are legitimate states; silently resolved is not.

Run those five against every timestamp in an incident before the timeline is drafted, and the review stops ending with "timestamps are hard." Timestamps are not hard. They are specific - and specificity, unlike hardness, can be checked.
